rv.q: Rachel Kavanaugh's revival of High Society turns out to be as uplifting as Kathleen Marshall.
Rachel Kavanaugh’s sleek production of High Society is an eminently welcome, frothy antidote to fretful times.
Nothing can obscure Porter's smart lyrics and the production's upbeat, feel-good nature.
See this for George, Kendal, Dyer and Lindsay.
It’s a very nice evening at the theatre - but it’s overshadowed by a production that was a proper event.
The songs are heavenly though – how could they not be? – with the perky Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, the romantic True Love and the divinely infectious Now You Have Jazz.
This revival of Cole Porter's beloved musical comedy is a triumphant reminder that golden age musicals, when staged with this much flair and heart, remain impossible to resist.

Happily, Rachel Kavanaugh’s production does almost everything right, matching Kiss Me, Kate and only fractionally short of Anything Goes, in being a lavish, big-hearted revival that never leaves its audience shortchanged: a swellegant, elegant party indeed.
In some ways, it is difficult to care too much about what is going on, especially if, like me, you’re not inclined to pay much (if any) attention to celebrity gossip.
But it's an enjoyable watch nonetheless, and a worthy addition to the dependably crowdpleasing Barbican Cole Porter canon.
Kavanaugh has created exactly the sort of glamorous, big-hearted musical audiences are craving now.
This show focuses more on visual spectacle than story but is a thoroughly enjoyable time that is timeless in its elegance.
This fun, fizzy, frivolous romp is the exact type of levity and escapism we need to see more of on the London stage.
Over the following two hours expectations are met and hopes realised.

At its best, the evening positively fizzes with champagne-bright sophistication, nowhere more so than in “Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?”, a number that perfectly captures the production’s blend of wit and style.
One of the most entertaining musicals you will see this summer, High Society will easily make you fall in love.
This production promises you a party, and on that it certainly delivers.
At the Barbican, director Rachel Kavanaugh employs and adapts Kopit’s version with great confidence, integrating a different selection of Porter’s hits.
What’s missing is emotional pull.
I never thought I was a fan of golden age musicals, but this production has proved me wrong - it is a pure joy-filled experience, which left a goofy smile on my face throughout.
High Society is an evening of pure theatrical pleasure.
High Society hits a sweet spot somewhere between uplifting and memorable, and will leave you humming the songs as you walk out into the night.
Overall, it's a nearly impeccable performance infused with classic-Broadway splendour, where plain entertainment is delivered in its finest form.
High Society fizzes with fun in a frolicking production which thrives both in performance and its music.
There's a brilliant feel-good effect that in itself makes this show worth seeing.
This production’s unexpected secret weapon is Ovenden as Lord’s ex-boyfriend Dexter who was clearly the best singer.

cn.t: Critics find this lavish Cole Porter revival a visually opulent, tuneful crowd-pleaser with stellar performances, though some note the flimsy plot and feel it doesn't quite match the Barbican's previous Porter triumphs like Anything Goes.
